title: Ford Bronco II
eyebrow: FORD BRONCO II · RANGER-BASED COMPACT SUV · 1984–1990
verdict: Ford put a roof on the new Ranger, cut the wheelbase to 94 inches and sold more than 760,000 of the result. It is light, narrow, simple and genuinely good on a tight trail, and it carries the heaviest safety file of any small 4x4 of its era. Buy one with your eyes open and drive it like what it is.

paragraphs: In March 1983 Ford introduced a second Bronco that had almost nothing to do with the first two. The Bronco II was the new Ranger compact pickup with a short enclosed wagon body where the bed would be, built alongside it at Louisville Assembly from January 1983 and sold as a 1984 model. It was roughly the size of the [[bronco/early-bronco|early Bronco]], nearly a foot shorter than Chevrolet's new S-10 Blazer, and it arrived the same year as the [[jeep/cherokee-xj|Jeep Cherokee XJ]] and the [[4runner/1st-gen|first 4Runner]]. MotorTrend liked it so much it decided XLT stood for "Xcellent Little Truck". Then the rollover numbers came in.

story.heading: 1984–85: A RANGER WITH A ROOF
paragraphs: Under the skin it was all Ranger: a ladder frame cut to a 94-inch wheelbase, Ford's Twin Traction Beam front suspension with a Dana 28 differential, coil springs and radius arms, and a leaf-sprung Ford 7.5-inch axle at the back. Wikipedia notes that nearly the whole driver's compartment came straight from the pickup. Every early truck was four-wheel drive, with a Borg-Warner 1350 transfer case, and power came from the German-built 2.8-liter Cologne V6: carbureted, 115 hp and 150 lb-ft. A Toyo Kogyo four-speed or a C5 three-speed automatic sent it rearward.

Ford sold it as a lifestyle object from the start. Its own marketing called it a vehicle for "men, single people, or young couples", the sort of John Wayne truck that made buyers feel they could conquer anything. The 1984 range already included an Eddie Bauer edition, which The Ranger Station calls the first Ford to wear the outdoor brand: two-tone paint over Light Desert Tan, a tan interior with pine-tree stitching, and Eddie Bauer luggage shipped to the buyer's house. For 1985 the four-speed became a five-speed, the A4LD four-speed automatic replaced the C5 from November 1984 builds, and power windows and locks finally arrived.

story.heading: 1986–90: FUEL INJECTION, 2WD AND A NEW FACE
paragraphs: For 1986 the 2.8 gave way to a fuel-injected 2.9-liter Cologne V6 with 140 hp and 170 lb-ft, and the push-button Touch-Drive electric transfer case appeared late in the year. A Mitsubishi 2.3-liter turbodiesel was listed as well; The Ranger Station says it was offered for 1986 only, Wikipedia says 1986 and 1987, and everyone agrees almost nobody bought it. Rear-wheel drive arrived too, though NHTSA's sales figures show the first 2WD trucks counted in the 1987 model year. Rear-wheel ABS became standard for 1987, and the XL Sport, with a brush guard, fog lamps and a tubular rear bumper, followed for 1988.

The 1989 facelift matched the restyled Ranger: new hood, fenders and front bumper, a new dashboard with the Touch-Drive buttons moved into it, and 3.6 more inches of overall length on the same wheelbase. The front-door vent windows disappeared, the 2.9 got stronger "89TM" cylinder heads, and Eddie Bauer trucks switched to Light Sandalwood lower paint. The last trucks brought the BW1354 transfer case on electric-shift models and, after November 1989, a Dana 35 front axle in place of the Dana 28. Production ended in early 1990. The Bronco II had been built for barely seven model years, while the [[bronco/full-size|full-size Bronco]] carried on until 1996.

story.heading: THE ROLLOVER RECORD
paragraphs: The trouble started before production. Automobile Magazine reports that Ford engineers calculated a stability index (a figure based on track width and center-of-gravity height) significantly lower than the S-10 Blazer's and slightly lower than the [[jeep/cj-7|Jeep CJ-7]]'s, that some test maneuvers were dropped for the drivers' safety, and that proposals to widen the track or lower the truck were mostly vetoed because they would have delayed the launch. In the summer of 1982 Ford's Office of General Counsel collected more than 100 documents on the truck's handling, 53 of which later turned out to be missing.

In March 1989 NHTSA opened an engineering analysis of 1984–89 Bronco IIs after its study of the Suzuki Samurai. That study counted 43 fatal single-vehicle Bronco II rollovers, or 19 per 100,000 vehicles, against 6 for the Samurai, 6 for the S-10 Blazer and Jimmy, and 2.5 for the Cherokee. Two months later Consumer Reports, published by Consumers Union, told readers to avoid the truck after it failed the magazine's emergency-handling tests. NHTSA closed its investigation on October 31, 1990, without a recall. Using its preferred measure, first-event single-vehicle rollovers per single-vehicle crash, the agency found the Bronco II similar to other small SUVs.

The argument never went away. NHTSA turned down a 1997 petition to reopen the case in May 1999. It repeated that the truck's rollover rate did not stand out, but added that its crashworthiness in rollovers was "a cause for concern", with a much higher share of occupants killed in first-event rollovers than in most peer vehicles. By 1997 about 260 people had died in Bronco II rollovers. Ford had paid $113 million to settle injury and death suits, and it offered a class settlement covering about 658,000 owners: new warning labels and manuals, $100 toward worn suspension parts and up to $200 for certain modifications. Ford has always maintained that driving and modifications, not design, caused the rollovers.

story.heading: THE EXPLORER, AND THE TRUCKS THAT SURVIVED
paragraphs: Ford replaced the Bronco II with the Ranger-based Explorer, introduced in March 1990 as a 1991 model with a 160-hp 4.0 V6 and the four doors the Bronco II never had. Even the two-door Explorer Sport was about a foot longer. According to PBS Frontline, Ford engineers ran an Explorer prototype through the same test the Bronco II had failed and saw it lift its wheels too. Thirty-odd years on, the surviving Bronco IIs are cheap, light and narrow, and owners build them around Explorer parts: Dana 35 front axles, 8.8 rear axles and 4.0 engines. Driven sensibly, kept low and treated as the narrow-track short-wheelbase truck it is, a Bronco II will go places a modern SUV won't fit.

callout.label: SIDEBAR · THE 2WD WITH A TRANSFER CASE
callout.title: The BW1359 "dummy" case
paragraphs: When Ford added a rear-drive Bronco II, it didn't redesign the drivetrain. Most 2WD trucks got the four-wheel-drive transmission, the same crossmember and rear driveshaft, and a Borg-Warner 1359 that looks like a transfer case but drives nothing. It passes power straight through to the rear axle and has a permanent seal where the front output would be. The Ranger Station's explanation is assembly-line efficiency: the short wheelbase made unique 2WD driveshafts and exhaust routing more trouble than a pass-through box.

Late in 1990 production some 2WD trucks finally got a true 2WD transmission with a bolt-on flange adapter instead. Owners note that some 1359s are dry and others contain ATF. The case is also why converting a 2WD Bronco II to 4WD is a popular, well-documented project. It only matters for safety because the 2WD truck had the worse record: Automobile Magazine cites IIHS figures of 3.78 rollover deaths per 10,000 rear-drive Bronco IIs in 1986–90, against 1.74 for the 4x4.

engineering_intro: The Bronco II is a first-generation Ranger under a short wagon body: a ladder frame with a 94-inch wheelbase and a 56.9-inch track, Twin Traction Beam independent front suspension on coil springs and radius arms, and leaf springs over a solid Ford 7.5-inch rear axle. Almost everything mechanical is shared with the 1983–92 Ranger and much of it with the 1991–94 Explorer, which is why the parts supply is good and the swap culture is strong.

engineering.v: Ladder frame · 94 in wheelbase · 56.9 in track
engineering.note: Shortened Ranger frame. Length grew from 158.3 in to 161.9 in with the 1989 facelift.

engineering.v: Twin Traction Beam, coil springs, radius arms
engineering.note: Two pivoting beams with a U-joint in the middle give independent travel. Camber changes as the suspension moves, so lifts need geometry correction.

engineering.v: Dana 28 TTB (1984–89) · Dana 35 TTB (built after Nov 1989)
engineering.note: Dana 28: 23-spline shafts, 6.625 in ring gear, rated for about 31 in tires. Dana 35: 27-spline, 7.56 in ring gear. In 1989 the ball joints moved from the beam to the knuckle.
Bronco II shafts are about 1-5/8 in wider than Ranger shafts on the passenger side. Ratios 3.45, 3.73 or 4.10; limited slip optional.

engineering.v: BW1350 (to 1990) · BW1354 (1990 electric shift) · BW1359 dummy (2WD)
engineering.note: Part-time, chain-drive, aluminum, 2.48:1 low range. Touch-Drive push buttons from late 1986, in the overhead console until 1988 and in the dash from 1989.

engineering.v: 2.8 Cologne V6 (1984–85) · 2.9 Cologne V6 EFI (1986–90) · 2.3 Mitsubishi turbodiesel (1986)
engineering.note: 2.8: 115 hp, carbureted, gear-driven cam. 2.9: 140 hp, chain-driven cam; bank-fire injection in 1986–87, sequential from 1988.

generations_table.note: TK4 four-speed or C5 three-speed automatic. BW1350 manual-shift transfer case, Dana 28 TTB, 7.5 rear. Standard, XLS, XLT and Eddie Bauer trims.
Five-speed manuals (TK5, FM145). A4LD four-speed automatic from November 1984 builds. Power window and lock group. Last XLS.

generations_table.engine: 2.9 Cologne V6 EFI · 2.3 Mitsubishi turbodiesel I4
generations_table.note: Fuel injection, 58 mm throttle body and EGR on 1986–87 2.9s. Touch-Drive electric shift arrives late in the year. The diesel sold poorly.
Rear ABS standard from 1987. 1988: sequential injection, FM146 and Mazda M5OD five-speeds, dual-solenoid A4LD from mid-year, XL Sport trim.
New nose and dash, 161.9 in long, no vent windows, improved 89TM heads. XLT Plus package. 1990: BW1354 on electric-shift trucks, Dana 35 TTB after November 1989.

buying_checks.head: Look for a cracked 2.9 head before anything else
buying_checks.body: The Ranger Station says early North American 2.9 heads lost material around the valve guides and rocker pedestals, and some cracked after a single overheat. Symptoms are white exhaust smoke when warm, clean spark plugs, low compression on a cylinder, and milky residue on the oil cap or dipstick (check it warm, since condensation looks similar). Rectangular rocker pedestals and an 89TM casting mean the improved heads have been fitted.

buying_checks.head: Listen to the valve train
buying_checks.body: On the 2.9, oil reaches the lifters, rocker shaft and rockers through the two center cam bearings, so slight bearing wear can starve the top end. Loud clatter, especially after a long highway run, warrants an oil-pressure check. The Ranger Station's figures are about 20 psi at warm idle and 55 psi at 2,000 rpm. Coolant in the oil from a cracked head quickly wipes out those bearings.

buying_checks.head: Hunt for water leaks and cowl rust
buying_checks.body: The cowl drains on 1984–88 trucks clog with leaves and rust through, putting water on the front carpet and in the glove box. The 1989–90 trucks got a mesh cowl. Every year leaks at the A-pillar and roof seam, the rear drip rail, the side-glass seals and behind the top of the hatch. A passenger floor that is always wet, rain or not, is usually the heater core.

buying_checks.head: Judge the A4LD, especially on 1985–87 trucks
buying_checks.body: The Ranger Station rates 1985–87 A4LDs as the weakest, with reliability improving after the dual-solenoid change in mid-1988. Heat is the main killer. Look for dark or burnt fluid, slow or missing overdrive, and hard or erratic shifts, which can mean a ruptured vacuum modulator. Fluid in the modulator's vacuum line confirms it, and so does white exhaust smoke from ATF being drawn into the engine.

buying_checks.head: Read the door sticker and the front axle
buying_checks.body: The certification label on the driver's door post carries axle and transmission codes, so you can confirm the ratio, a limited-slip rear and the original gearbox. Dana 28 axles have 12 cover bolts and date codes starting with E; the Dana 35 has a 10-bolt cover and F codes. Only 1990 trucks built after November 1989 left the factory with a Dana 35.

buying_checks.head: Check the TTB and the hubs
buying_checks.body: Uneven tire wear points to tired beam pivot bushings, ball joints or radius-arm bushings, or a lift without camber correction. The Ranger Station advises checking the beam pivot bushings whenever the front end is apart. The factory automatic locking hubs become unreliable with age, and owners usually replace them with manual hubs.

buying_checks.head: Is it really a 4x4?
buying_checks.body: A 2WD Bronco II often has what looks like a transfer case, the BW1359 pass-through, so look for a front driveshaft, a front differential and a shifter or Touch-Drive buttons. Also look for 2WD-to-4WD conversions, which are common. Check the quality of the swapped axle, the driveshafts and the transfer-case linkage.

buying_checks.head: Run the recalls and question the modifications
buying_checks.body: NHTSA lists campaigns for locking-hub cams (1984), seat-belt anchors (1984), fuel lines and an EEC harness short (1986), handling-warning stickers on the sun visor (1987) and missing front wheel-bearing keys (1989). Ford blamed many rollovers on unsafe modifications. Treat a tall lift on a narrow 94-inch truck with suspicion and ask how it was engineered.

repairs.title: Replace cracked 2.9 cylinder heads
repairs.symptoms: White smoke when warm, clean spark plugs, low compression on one or more cylinders, coolant loss with no external leak, or milky "snot" on a warm dipstick or oil cap.
repairs.fix: Stop driving it: The Ranger Station warns that coolant in the oil destroys the crank bearings and turns a head job into a rebuild. Drain the oil and coolant, pull the intake and both heads, and have them magnafluxed to confirm the crack. Fit the improved 1989-on heads (89TM castings with rectangular rocker pedestals) or aftermarket heads from World Products. Torque the head bolts in three steps: 22 lb-ft, then 51–55 lb-ft, then a further 90 degrees. Tighten the intake manifold to 15–18 lb-ft in five steps and retorque it after warm-up. Old valve covers with turned-down flanges tend to leak on the newer heads, so use later covers with turned-up flanges. Change the oil again after the first run.
repairs.tools: Torque wrench and angle gauge · gasket scraper · compression tester · machine-shop magnaflux.

parts.name: Cylinder head gasket set, 1988 Bronco II 2.9

repairs.title: Replace 2.8 valve stem seals without pulling the heads
repairs.cost: Under the price of a set of seals plus an air adapter
repairs.symptoms: Blue smoke on start-up or overrun, and oil consumption on a high-mileage 2.8. The Ranger Station says the original rubber valve seals deteriorate and leak oil into the cylinders.
repairs.fix: Remove a valve cover, then the spark plug and wire for the cylinder you're working on. Loosen the rocker-shaft stand bolts two turns at a time from the ends toward the middle, lift off the shaft and oil baffle, and remove both pushrods. Screw an air adapter into the 14 mm plug hole and pressurize the cylinder to hold the valves shut; if they won't hold, the seats are damaged and the head has to come off. Compress the spring, remove the keepers, retainer and spring, replace the seal and reassemble. Repeat on each cylinder, then reset the valve lash (0.014 in intake, 0.016 in exhaust).
repairs.tools: Air compressor · spark-plug-hole air adapter · valve spring compressor · feeler gauges · torque wrench.

repairs.title: Reseal leaking valve covers
repairs.symptoms: Oil weeping down the heads onto the exhaust manifolds, a burning-oil smell after a drive, an oily engine bay.
repairs.fix: The Ranger Station calls Cologne valve-cover leaks messy but not dangerous, apart from rare fires when a lot of oil reaches the exhaust. Remove the intake plumbing or wiring that's in the way, unbolt the covers, clean both sealing surfaces completely and fit Fel-Pro rubber or Fel-Pro Blue gaskets. If the engine has the improved 1989-on heads, use the later covers with turned-up flanges, because old-style covers leak on the flatter surface. Tighten the bolts evenly and only lightly.
repairs.tools: Sockets and extensions · gasket scraper · brake cleaner.

repairs.title: Replace or relocate the TFI ignition module
repairs.cost: Parts plus a donor heat sink
repairs.symptoms: The engine dies or won't restart when hot, then runs again after it cools down, without leaving a trace of the fault.
repairs.fix: The Thick Film Ignition module is mounted on the distributor, one of the hottest places under the hood. Disconnect the battery and remove the two screws with a thin-wall 7/32 in (5.5 mm) socket or a T20, depending on the screw. Slide the module down before pulling it away from the distributor, or it won't come off. For a permanent fix, The Ranger Station shows how to mount the module remotely on a finned heat sink from a 1989–95 Mercury Cougar or an Aerostar, trimming fins to clear the Ranger's connectors. Don't paint the heat sink. On the 2.8, owners also convert to Duraspark, GM HEI or aftermarket ignition.
repairs.tools: Thin-wall 7/32 in (5.5 mm) socket or ignition-module wrench · T20 driver · basic hand tools.

repairs.title: Service the A4LD, replace the modulator and add a cooler
repairs.symptoms: Dark or burnt-smelling fluid, slipping, no overdrive, hard or erratic shifts, a missing 1–2 shift or third gear, or white exhaust smoke from ATF being drawn through a ruptured modulator.
repairs.fix: Drop the pan, change the filter, clean the pan and refill with Mercon-type ATF (The Ranger Station recommends Mercon V as the modern replacement; total capacity is about 9.5 quarts). Pull the vacuum hose from the modulator: fluid in the hose means the diaphragm has failed, and you can confirm it with a vacuum gauge before fitting a new one. Heat is the main enemy of the A4LD, so fit an auxiliary cooler in the return line to supplement the radiator cooler. On 1988-on dual-solenoid units, test the 3-pin connector if overdrive or lock-up is missing.
repairs.tools: Drain pan · sockets · gasket scraper · hand vacuum pump or gauge · funnel.

repairs.title: Refresh the TTB front end and set camber
repairs.symptoms: Tires wearing on the inside or outside edge, clunks over bumps, wandering, or play when you rock the wheel top to bottom.
repairs.fix: Support the frame and unload the front axle. Inspect the beam pivot bushings where each beam meets its frame bracket, the radius-arm bushings, the ball joints and the tie-rod ends, and replace whatever is worn. Camber on a TTB is set with an offset cam bushing around the upper ball joint, and the right bushing brings worn or lifted beams back into spec. On 1984–88 axles the ball joints are in the beam; from 1989 they moved to the knuckle. If the truck is lifted, check that it has drop brackets for the beam pivots and radius arms and a dropped pitman arm. The Ranger Station warns against kits that lower the passenger beam pivot with a bolt-on drop plate, because the differential can strike it. Finish with a proper alignment.
repairs.tools: Jack and stands · ball-joint press · pickle fork · large sockets · torque wrench.

parts.name: TTB axle (beam) pivot bushing, 1988 Bronco II

repairs.title: Find and seal water leaks
repairs.symptoms: A wet front floor, water in the glove box, drips from the headliner just behind the windshield, a wet cargo carpet, fogged windows and a musty smell.
repairs.fix: First rule out the heater core: a passenger floor that stays wet without rain is usually coolant, and the core sits behind an easy-to-remove panel under the dash. On 1984–88 trucks, clear the cowl drains and seal the cowl-to-firewall seam. Small holes can be sealed through the access covers, but rusted cowls mean drilling out spot welds. For the A-pillar and roof seam, the rear drip rail and the area above the hatch, dig out the cracked factory seam sealer and apply new sealer (silicone is only a temporary fix). Leaking side glass has to come out: remove the trim, unbolt the glass, cut the old seal with piano wire with a helper and reseal it with tar ribbon. Don't force it, because the glass breaks easily and is expensive.
repairs.tools: Trim tools · seam sealer · tar ribbon · piano wire · drill (for cowl repairs).

repairs.title: Fix a liftgate that won't release
repairs.symptoms: You turn the handle, feel resistance and a click, and the tension lets go without the gate opening, or it only opens if you push on the handle while turning it.
repairs.fix: This is the Bronco II Corral fix for a worn release catch. Remove the inner trim panel (screws around the edge, then slide it forward and pop the push-pins). Remove the two 9 mm nuts and the retaining plate and pull the handle out. Take out the 7/32 in screw on the end of the handle, lift off the latch arm, put a 9/16 in washer under it as a shim and refit the arm the right way round (the nub faces away from the word "Gate"). Test the gate before refitting the panel. If you're stuck in the meantime, you can open the gate from inside by pulling one of the latch rods toward the center.
repairs.tools: Phillips screwdriver · 1/4 in ratchet · 9 mm and 7/32 in sockets · push-pin pliers.

faq.q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
faq.a: Stock was 205/75R15, about 27 inches tall. The Ranger Station shows a stock-height Bronco II on 31x10.50R15s with trimmed fenders, and its rule of thumb is that 31s need about 1.5 inches of lift plus fender trimming. 32x11.50R15s have fitted on a 1.5-inch lift with the bottom rear corner of the front fender trimmed. Remember that the Dana 28 front axle is rated for about 31-inch tires.

faq.q: 2.8 or 2.9: which engine should I want?
faq.a: The carbureted 2.8 (1984–85) is simple, with gear-driven cam timing, but it makes 115 hp, burns oil through worn valve seals, and its aging feedback carburetor tends to misbehave. The injected 2.9 (1986–90) makes 140 hp and 170 lb-ft. Its early heads crack and its top end is sensitive to cam-bearing wear, but 1989-on 89TM heads largely cured the cracking. A well-maintained 2.9 with the later heads is the pick.

Yes. Ford offered a Mitsubishi 2.3-liter turbodiesel four-cylinder. The Ranger Station's specification table lists it for 1986 only, while Wikipedia and a Hemmings history say 1986–87. Everyone agrees it was slow and sold poorly, so factory diesel Bronco IIs are rare today.

faq.q: Is the Bronco II really more likely to roll over?
faq.a: NHTSA twice declined to call it defective, in 1990 and 1999, because its rollover rate per single-vehicle crash was similar to its peers. The same 1999 review called its crashworthiness in rollovers "a cause for concern": a much larger share of occupants died in first-event rollovers than in most comparable SUVs. IIHS figures cited by Automobile put the 1986–90 rear-drive truck at 3.78 rollover deaths per 10,000 vehicles and the 4x4 at 1.74. It's a narrow, short truck, so drive it accordingly and be careful about adding height.

faq.q: Dana 28 or Dana 35: what do I have and does it matter?
faq.a: Almost every Bronco II has the Dana 28 TTB: 23-spline shafts, a 6.625-inch ring gear and little aftermarket support for gears or lockers now. Only 1990 trucks built from November 1989 got the Dana 35, with 27-spline shafts and a 7.56-inch ring gear. Count the cover bolts (12 on a Dana 28, 10 on a Dana 35) or read the date code. Serious builders swap in a Dana 35 from an Explorer.

faq.q: Can a 2WD Bronco II be converted to 4WD?
faq.a: Yes. It's a common, well-documented job because most 2WD trucks already have the 4WD-style transmission and a BW1359 pass-through case in the transfer-case position. You need a front TTB axle, a working transfer case and shifter, a front driveshaft and the matching parts. Late 1990 2WD trucks with a true 2WD transmission and a flange adapter need more work.

Manuals are the safe bet: Ford fitted TK4 (1984), TK5 and FM145 (1985–87), and FM146 or Mazda M5OD five-speeds (1988–90). The M5OD runs on Mercon ATF and tends to leak from rubber plugs in its top cover, which owners replace with steel cup plugs (Dorman 555-108). The Ranger Station rates the 1985–87 A4LD automatic as the weakest and says it improved from mid-1988. Whatever you have, add an auxiliary cooler to an A4LD.

According to The Ranger Station's specification pages, the 2.9 takes 5.0 quarts of oil with the filter and the 2.8 takes 5. The BW1350 and BW1354 transfer cases take about 2 quarts of ATF (Dexron III/Mercon, Mercon V or Mercon LV, never gear oil). The A4LD takes Mercon (Mercon V is the modern replacement), about 9.5 quarts. The 7.5 rear takes 75W-80 or 80W-90 hypoid oil, about 5 pints, with 2 oz of friction modifier for a limited slip. Check grades in the owner's manual.

faq.q: What engine swaps do people do?
faq.a: The most common is the 4.0 V6 from an Explorer or later Ranger, which shares Cologne family roots with the 2.9, and The Ranger Station has wiring guides for 4.0 swaps into both early and late dashes. The 5.0 V8 is the bigger project. Bring a Trailer has sold several swapped trucks, including 4.0-powered 1988 and 1989 Bronco IIs and a 302-powered 1989.
faq.src: THE RANGER STATION · BRING A TRAILER

faq.q: How is it related to the Ranger and the Explorer?
faq.a: It is a first-generation Ranger underneath, built on the same Louisville line with the same TTB front end, 7.5 rear and Cologne V6s, and nearly the same driver's compartment. The Explorer replaced it for 1991, still Ranger-based but bigger, with four doors available and a 4.0 V6. Its Dana 35, 8.8 rear axle and 4.0 are now the standard Bronco II upgrades.

Not much yet, which is part of the appeal. On Bring a Trailer in 2025–26, most stock XLTs and Eddie Bauers sold for $6,450 to $15,750. A 9,000-mile 1989 Eddie Bauer reached $28,550 in April 2025, and a 1989 Eddie Bauer five-speed was bid to $12,000 in August 2026 without selling.

faq.q: Which years are the best to buy?
faq.a: 1989–1990. The Ranger Station says the 2.9's cylinder heads were redesigned for 1989 (look for '89TM' castings and rectangular rocker pedestals), largely ending the cracking that plagues 1986–88 engines, and that 1989-on A4LD automatics are noticeably better than the 1985–87 units its builder's guide says to stay away from. A late-1990 4x4 may also have the stronger Dana 35 front axle. If you do buy a 1986–88, check the oil for coolant, or for proof the heads have been swapped.

mods.why: TTB lifts use taller coils, drop brackets for the beam pivots and radius arms, a dropped pitman arm and rear add-a-leafs or blocks. The Ranger Station's builder guides name James Duff and Skyjacker, and warns against bolt-on drop plates for the passenger beam pivot.
Bigger tires on a Bronco II mostly come down to fender trimming. Cut-out flares are how the 33- and 35-inch builds on The Ranger Station clear without huge lifts.
The Dana 28 is good for about 31-inch tires, so builders swap in an Explorer Dana 35 TTB in front and often an Explorer 8.8 in the rear, then regear both to suit the tires.

who.name: The Ranger Station — Dana 28 to Dana 35 swap

mods.why: The Ranger Station's builder guide lists a Lock-Right (1830-LR) for the 7.5 rear. The Dana 28 front has little support left, which is one more reason to swap to a Dana 35.
A 4.0 V6 from an Explorer is the classic Bronco II upgrade, and a 5.0 V8 is the ambitious one. Adapters, mounts and wiring are well documented.
A small, light truck still needs a winch and real recovery points. The Ranger Station's builder guide sizes a winch at 1.5 times the gross vehicle weight.

baseline_service.intro: Most Bronco IIs for sale are 35-plus years old and have passed through several cheap owners, so baseline everything. On a 2.9, the cooling system is a priority, because The Ranger Station says one overheat can crack an early head, and it calls synthetic oil and good cooling maintenance essential. On a 4x4, service the transfer case with ATF, not gear oil, and inspect the TTB front end.

items.note: Check oil pressure if the valve train is noisy: The Ranger Station quotes about 20 psi at warm idle and 55 psi at 2,000 rpm for the 2.9. Look for milky residue under the filler cap.

items.spec: 7.2 qt (with A/C) / 7.8 qt (without A/C) per The Ranger Station · coolant type [CONFIRM IN MANUAL]
items.interval: Flush at purchase; fit a new thermostat and hoses if their age is unknown
items.note: The single most important item on a 2.9. Pressure-test the system and check the radiator, fan clutch and water pump.

items.spec: Motorcraft AWSF-42C gapped 0.044 in · timing 10° BTDC · firing order 1-4-2-5-3-6
items.note: These specs are listed for both the 2.8 and the 2.9. On the 2.8, check that the distributor hold-down and rotor screws are tight, because loose ones change the timing.

items.interval: Inspect at purchase; carry a spare
items.note: Heat makes it fail intermittently on a hot engine. Relocating it to a heat sink is a well-documented fix.

items.interval: Replace at purchase; check the air filter after dusty trails
items.note: The 2.9 is fuel-injected (30–40 psi fuel pressure per The Ranger Station), so relieve the pressure before opening the lines. Recall 87V-139 added retainer clips to spring-lock fuel couplings on 1986–87 trucks.

items.spec: Mercon ATF (Mercon V as the modern replacement) · ≈ 9.5 qt total
items.interval: Pan drop and filter at purchase
items.note: A pan drop replaces only part of the fluid. Check the vacuum modulator line for ATF and add an auxiliary cooler. 1985–87 units are the most fragile.

items.spec: TK4, TK5 and M5OD: Mercon ATF · FM145 and FM146: [CONFIRM IN MANUAL]
items.note: Identify the gearbox from the TRANS code on the door-post label. On an M5OD, replace the three rubber top-cover plugs with steel cup plugs (Dorman 555-108 or Dana 219-3052), because leaks there can run it low.

items.spec: ≈ 2 qt ATF: Dexron III/Mercon, Mercon V or Mercon LV per the factory manual, NOT gear oil
items.note: The 2WD BW1359 pass-through case is a special case: some contain ATF and some are dry. On Touch-Drive trucks, test every mode from the buttons.

parts.name: Transfer case output seal, 1988 Bronco II

items.spec: Hypoid gear oil SAE 80W or 90W · The Ranger Station lists 2 qt (Dana 28) / 3 qt (Dana 35) [CONFIRM AT FILL PLUG]
items.interval: Change at purchase and after deep water
items.note: Check the slip-yoke seal on the long side and the axle vent.

items.spec: Hypoid gear oil SAE 75W-80 or 80W-90 · ≈ 5 pints · add 2 oz friction modifier for a limited slip
items.note: The axle code on the door-post label tells you the ratio and whether it's a limited slip.
Check that the bearing-adjusting nut retaining keys are present (recall 89V-109 covered trucks that left the factory without them). Replace failing automatic hubs with manual hubs.

items.spec: Beam pivot bushings · radius-arm bushings · ball joints · tie-rod ends
items.note: Uneven tire wear is the tell. Fix camber with offset bushings, not by ignoring it.
Front discs and rear drums, with rear-wheel ABS from 1987. On manual trucks the hydraulic clutch is worth bleeding at the same time.
